units.translation: 18. πυκνὰ δὲ λαυκα〈νίης〉: of the throat, the windpipe, through which the breath is drawn down. κουρίξ means on the temple, on the head; they often use it for plucking out hairs. LGmSmP
7 Hesychius κουρίξ. κ. αἰνυμένους Eustathius 966, 63. 1924, 12
6 λαυκανίας in L(P) : omitted in GS
7 καταφέρεται in GS : φέρεται in LP : ἀνέρχεται in A
8 πολλάκις κτλ. in LP : omitted in GS
23-24. πτερόεις δέ οἱ: as it were light; she was lifted from her former reasoning, her soul quickly changed, it was turned to cheerfulness.
9 προτέρου in P : πρότερον in L
35. διειλυσθεῖσα: having secretly gone out of the house, having run away, having fled.
36. ληιάς: captive, spear-won.
38. ἀηθέσσουσα: being unaccustomed. δύης means of misery.
42. ἀοιδαῖς: with enchantments through drugs. Lm (P)
16 sch. Call. H. III 12 Poll. VII 62 Hesychius πέζα. ᾤα Συν. π. ὤ. (335, 7. 420, 17 Ba. Phot. Suid.) Et. M. 820, 6 Et. Gud. 573, 44 Sturz Eust. 146, 29. 1828, 55
46. πέζαν: the edge of the tunic, which we call ᾤα; for formerly a sheepskin was sewn on to prevent it from being worn away.
52. ἀμφί τε δυσπαλέας: difficult and evil. Or those that spring up from the earth for harm; for the destructive are more numerous than the wholesome. Or those that are hard to injure.
18 Et. Gen. (AB) δυσπαλέας ῥίζας: IV 52. those that spring up badly, from πάλλω. Or those that come into being with difficulty (see above). Apollonius (Ἀπ. in A, omitted in B).
20 σιν- in W : γιν-
54. τὴν δὲ νέον Τιτηνίς: Helios and Selene are children of Hyperion the Titan and Theia, as Hesiod says (Theog. 371): 'Theia bore Helios and bright Selene.'
23 Ἡ. τε μέγαν λ. in Hesiod
55. φοιταλέην: mad, going about madly; for φοῖτος is said for madness. And Euphorion (fg 108 Scheidw.):
24 Hesychius Suda φοῖτος
Perhaps for this reason we also call courtesans φοιτάδες.
1 διὰ in L : δ’ ἀνὰ in P ἄδην Valckenaer : ἄλην

57-58. οὐκ ἄρ’ ἐγὼ μούνη μετὰ Λάτμιον: Latmus is a mountain of Caria, where there is a cave in which Endymion used to dwell. There is also a city called Heracleia. Selene is said to descend into this cave to Endymion. About the love of Selene Sappho (fg inc. lib. 83 Lobel = 134 B. III 132) and Nicander in the second book of the Europeia (fg 24 Schn.) tell the story.

Hesiod (fg 11 Rz.²) says that Endymion was the son of Aethlius, son of Zeus, and Calyce, and that he received from Zeus the gift to be the steward of his own death, whenever he wished to perish 〈...〉; and Peisander (16 fg 7 J.) and Acusilaus (2 fg 36 J.) and Pherecydes (3 fg 121 J.) and Nicander in the second book of the Aetolica (fg 6 Schn.) and Theopompus the epic poet. They say that he was †Spartiate†, but others say Elean; Ibycus in the first book (fg 44 B. III 249) says that he was king of Elis.
